# D-7TDUEHUOFXPTSQCE The site is generated by chirp from the repo's Markdown and published from main on every green push and after releases

## Context
chirp needed a public site saying what it is and how to get it, and BR wanted the repo's way of working (dev-proc) shown too. A site written by hand would be a second copy of docs that already exist in the binary and the skill. D-ME7B5XOAG245FN65 first published it after each tag's release; BR then asked for a build of main that can be downloaded between releases (D-6NWFV37OBOERI3AF), and decided that the whole site follows main as well.

## Decision
The site is built by chirp itself from the repo's Markdown: README, CHANGELOG, the help topics, and SKILL.md as-is behind a short intro, plus an examples page that links to commits. It is published to GitHub Pages after every push to main whose CI succeeds, after each tag's release, and by manual runs on main. A run publishes only if its commit is main's tip, checked when the run is planned and again when the deploy starts. Each page's footer names the commit and the chirp version it was built from.

## Why
Rendering the sources that already exist means the site cannot say something the binary's own docs do not. Jekyll or Hugo would add a second toolchain to a project whose point is needing nothing but chirp; bundling md4c (D-UCQGXYU3CLHRAYIT) made that unnecessary. Commit links are immutable, so the examples age but do not drift. Failing the build on an unresolved link or an unknown commit makes a broken site a red run instead of a 404 someone finds later.
- **Releases only, as before:** rejected. Docs and the try page then lag main by a whole release, while the main build beside them already carries the change. With the footer naming version and commit, a reader can see which state a page describes, so publishing from main costs no clarity.
- **A build trigger of its own on push:** rejected. The pages build reuses the binaries that CI built, compared and ran, as a release does, so it runs after CI and does not build the eight-binary matrix twice.
- **Concurrency alone to keep an old build from replacing a new one:** not enough. CI runs finish in an order that differs from the pushes, so a run publishes only if its commit is still the tip of main. The tag's release run too: when main has moved on, the newer deploy already carries the release, and the tag's older site must not replace it.
- **A concurrency group on the whole workflow or on the build:** rejected. A run that publishes nothing would take a place in the queue, and an older run joining could replace a newer waiting one. The one queue is on the deploy job, whose first step checks the tip.

## Consequences
- A doc change reaches the site at the next green push to main.
- A new source file or page is added in `site/build.janet`, not by dropping a file somewhere.
- Raw HTML in the sources is rendered; they are the repo's own files, so this is trusted input.
- A broken push to main publishes nothing, so the site keeps describing the last green one.
